clue.text: Bottled beer in bar, now drunk by the French

indicators.note: drunk suggests something reeling and mixed up, so the letters of bar and now are rearranged

parts.note: le is the French masculine word for the

explanation.surface: A drinker in a pub finishes a bottle while the French look on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' turns BAR NOW into BROWNA; LE, French for 'the', follows.
explanation.definitionFit: This dark, sweetish English beer is usually sold in bottles rather than on draught.

clue.text: Composer, fine composer

parts.note: Lionel Bart was the English composer of the musical Oliver!
OK means fine

explanation.surface: A composer is praised as a fine composer.
explanation.walkthrough: BART is Lionel Bart, the London songwriter behind the musical Oliver!
explanation.definitionFit: Béla Bartók was a Hungarian twentieth-century composer.

clue.text: Theatre now running top film

indicators.note: running means flowing freely, so the letters of theatre and now are rearranged

parts.note: the top or head of something is its front

explanation.surface: A theatre now shows a top film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running' looks like a show's run, but it turns THEATRE NOW into ONTHEWATER.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the 1954 Elia Kazan movie starring Marlon Brando as a dockworker.

clue.text: Name only synthetic material

indicators.note: synthetic means artificially made up, so the letters of only are reworked

explanation.surface: A fabric advertised only by its synthetic material name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'synthetic material' looks like the definition, but 'synthetic' scrambles ONLY.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a strong artificial fibre used for stockings and fabric.

clue.text: Reportedly praise exercise book

indicators.note: reportedly means the words for praise and exercise are spoken, giving sound-alike spellings

parts.note: to laud is to praise, and gym is physical exercise or PE

explanation.surface: Someone praises a school exercise book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exercise book' reads as a school notebook; in non-rhotic British speech LAUD sounds like LORD and GYM like JIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Jim is a novel by Joseph Conrad published in 1900.

clue.text: TT race practice

parts.note: TT stands for teetotal, and a teetotal person or place is dry
to race is to run

explanation.surface: Riders get some practice before the Isle of Man motorcycle race.
explanation.walkthrough: TT looks like the Isle of Man Tourist Trophy motorbike race, but here it means teetotal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal held before the real event is a trial session.

clue.text: A journey — set off after several drinks

indicators.note: after places the word for set off behind the round of drinks

parts.note: a round is a set of drinks bought for a group
to trip an alarm is to set it off

explanation.surface: Someone heads off on a journey after a few drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set off' looks like 'depart', but it is TRIP as in tripping a switch.
explanation.definitionFit: An outing there and back again is an excursion.

clue.text: A sure thing with Cary Grant in it, based loosely around church

indicators.note: around says the jumbled letters go round the abbreviation for church
based loosely suggests a story only loosely drawn from the original, so the letters of Cary Grant in it are rearranged

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A film starring Cary Grant, loosely based on a church story, is a safe bet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'based loosely' mixes CARYGRANTINIT, which wraps CE (Church of England).
explanation.definitionFit: In horse-race slang, a runner certain to win is a dead cert, a sure bet.

clue.text: Around noon, son seen playing in folly

indicators.note: Around says the jumbled letters go round the abbreviation for noon
playing means fooling about, so the letters of son and seen are jumbled

explanation.surface: Around midday a son is seen playing the fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' mixes SON SEEN into NOSENSE, which goes 'Around' N.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolish talk or behaviour is rubbish or absurdity.

clue.text: Snakes, excellent specimens

explanation.surface: A naturalist praises some fine snakes in a collection.
explanation.definitionFit: Rattlesnakes are informally called this, and in old slang a ripper or corker of a thing is one too.

clue.text: King's horse caught by a knight

parts.note: a dun is a horse of greyish-brown colour
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A monarch's steed is seized by a knight on the battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after King is 'is', a link; the king is Shakespeare's Scottish monarch murdered in Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Duncan is the Scottish monarch killed by Macbeth in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Stylish young woman? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite means the word is not complete, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: chick is slang for a young woman

explanation.surface: Is a young woman stylish? Not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' drops the final K from CHICK.
explanation.definitionFit: Chic means elegant and fashionable.

clue.text: Once a warring Indian, say

indicators.note: warring parts are in conflict and disarray, so the letters of once a are jumbled

explanation.surface: A Native American who once fought in battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian' suggests a person; it is the Indian Ocean, one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indian is one of the great seas of the world, an example of the class.

clue.text: Poet can no more, we hear

parts.note: can and john are both slang words for a lavatory

indicators.note: we hear says the word for no more is heard rather than seen, giving a sound-alike spelling

parts.note: something that is no more is finished, done

explanation.surface: A writer laments that they can write no more.
explanation.walkthrough: JOHN is American slang for a toilet, like 'can'.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne was a metaphysical poet and Dean of St Paul's in the seventeenth century.

clue.text: Wild, organised party at end of term

parts.note: to organise an event is to run it; ran is the past tense
a do is a party or celebration

indicators.note: end of picks out only the final letter of the word term

explanation.surface: Students hold a wild end-of-term party.
explanation.definitionFit: Something haphazard and without pattern can be called wild or arbitrary.

clue.text: Diane's one who cultivates source of strong spirit?

parts.note: Di is short for Diane, so Diane's becomes Di's
a tiller is someone who tills, or cultivates, the land

explanation.surface: Diane's gardener is the source of her strong spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'source of strong spirit' is a whimsical way to describe a maker of whisky or gin.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm or person producing whisky or vodka is where hard liquor comes from.

clue.text: Body detailed to capture a capital city

indicators.note: to capture means to hold the letter a inside the shortened body
de-tailed means having its tail, its last letter, cut off

parts.note: a carcass is a dead body

explanation.surface: A corpse sent to take over a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' looks like 'assigned', but read de-tailed: CARCASS loses its last S, giving CARCAS, which then takes in A.
explanation.definitionFit: Caracas is the capital of Venezuela.

clue.text: Child on board earlier ship

indicators.note: on board says the child is carried inside the word for earlier

parts.note: sooner means earlier

explanation.surface: A child was on board a ship earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' means carried within: CH goes inside SOONER.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is a sailing vessel with two or more masts.

clue.text: Check complicated lease in part of London

parts.note: CH is the chess abbreviation for check

indicators.note: complicated means twisted and involved, so the letters of lease are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tenant checks a complicated lease on a London property.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea is a wealthy district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Chelsea is a district of west London on the Thames.

clue.text: A number climbing spotted deer

indicators.note: climbing in a down clue means the word for a number is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: six is a number

explanation.surface: A herd of spotted deer climbs a hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'climbing' reverses SIX to XIS.
explanation.definitionFit: The axis or chital is a white-spotted deer of India.

clue.text: Sports official member and I ducked in Yorkshire river

indicators.note: ducked in means plunged into the water, so the letters go inside the river

parts.note: the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A referee and a politician get thrown into a Yorkshire river.
explanation.walkthrough: The URE is a river in North Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket or tennis official who rules on play is a referee or judge.

clue.text: Steal the show, winning leg

parts.note: a player who is winning is up
a leg of a journey is a stage

explanation.surface: An athlete steals the show by winning a leg of the race.
explanation.definitionFit: To outshine others and draw attention from them is to overshadow them.

clue.text: Flinch in fear on bend

parts.note: re means on or concerning
a coil is a bend or loop

explanation.surface: Someone flinches in fear at a bend in the road.
explanation.definitionFit: To shrink back in horror or dismay is to start or jump back.

clue.text: Out of bounds in round — last of golf films shot includes it

parts.note: O is round in shape

indicators.note: last of takes only the final letter of the word golf
includes means the jumbled letters hold the word it within them
shot means wrecked, so the letters of films are rearranged

explanation.surface: A golfer, ending a round, finds the course out of bounds to camera crews.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' scrambles FILMS to FLIMS, which 'includes' IT, giving FLIMITS after O and F.
explanation.definitionFit: A place where entry is forbidden is barred or prohibited.

clue.text: Mere used by British poet

parts.note: a mere is a lake or pond

explanation.surface: A British poet writes about a mere, as Romantic poets do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mere' looks like 'only', but it is a noun for a small lake.
explanation.definitionFit: William Blake was an English Romantic poet and artist.

clue.text: Read novel written by key wartime aviator

indicators.note: written by places the rearranged letters after the key

parts.note: B is a musical key

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so the letters of read are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wartime pilot writes a novel in a particular musical key.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas BADER was a British fighter pilot of the Second World War who flew despite losing both legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Douglas Bader was an RAF fighter pilot in the Second World War.

clue.text: Silly person, old one in trouble

indicators.note: in trouble suggests the letters are disturbed and mixed up

explanation.surface: A foolish old person gets into difficulties.
explanation.definitionFit: Noodle is informal for a fool or simpleton.

clue.text: Dance enthusiast going round with energy

indicators.note: going round says the enthusiast encircles the word for with

parts.note: a fan is an enthusiast
and means with or plus
go means energy or vigour

explanation.surface: A keen dancer twirls round energetically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going' tempts as GO, but 'going round' is the container; the GO comes from 'energy'.
explanation.definitionFit: The fandango is a lively Spanish courtship dance in triple time.

clue.text: Soldiers go and come back

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a go is a turn

explanation.surface: Soldiers head off to war and then return home.
explanation.walkthrough: RE, the Royal Engineers, is a regiment of the British Army.
explanation.definitionFit: To go back to a place is to revisit it.

clue.text: Beryl at a moving Pinter play

indicators.note: moving means shifting about, so the letters of Beryl at a are rearranged

explanation.surface: An actress named Beryl gives a moving performance in a Pinter play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' looks like praise for the acting.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Pinter wrote this 1978 drama about an adulterous affair.
